title: IPO Base
teaches: The IPO base as we trade it: a new issue's first rest under its own IPO high, light volume on the pullbacks, never bought on the listing day or in the listing week, the buy is the trade through the IPO high at market in regular hours and no more than 4% past it, the stop sits a few cents under the breakout day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

steps: KRMN, 2025. Listed in February, it rests under its IPO high of 57.32 for 6.8 weeks, 22% deep, in a hot theme.

A bounce up off the listing-day low
A spike that doubles in only a few weeks

wrong.A spike that doubles in only a few weeks: That is a run, not a rest. The base is the pause under the high, and IBD says to avoid a new issue right after a massive run.

Yes, a clean and tight base
Yes, but at half size
No; wait one day, then buy it
questions.answer: No; wait until after the report
questions.why: No. We make no new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report, and this report is 2 sessions away. A new issue's first report can come soon after listing, so check the date. The rule covers only those 3 sessions before the report.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date on a new issue. Inside 3 sessions, wait.

wrong.Yes, a clean and tight base: A clean base does not lift the earnings rule. There is no new buy in the 3 sessions before a report.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: The rule is no new buy in that window, not a smaller one.
wrong.No; wait one day, then buy it: Tomorrow is still inside the 3 sessions before the report. Wait until after it.

questions.story: The base is tight under the IPO high and breaks out this morning. The first quarterly report is in 2 sessions.
questions.simple: No. The report is 2 sessions away, inside the 3-session no-buy window, so wait until after it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B22
fixed before: variety rewrite 2026-11-10

questions.q: A stock listed 6 weeks ago rests under its high. Which card applies?
choices: The cup with handle card
The IPO base card
The flat base card
questions.answer: The IPO base card
questions.why: The IPO base card. The listing date decides: an IPO base is a young stock's first rest under its post-listing high inside its first year.
questions.lesson_line: Many IPO bases look like cups. The listing date decides which card applies.

wrong.The cup with handle card: A cup needs a stock with a trading history. A stock listed 6 weeks ago has none.
wrong.The flat base card: A flat base is for a seasoned leader, not a stock listed 6 weeks ago.

questions.q: Which card is it?
choices: None; no 200-day
The flat card
The IPO base card
The VCP card
questions.answer: The IPO base card
questions.why: The IPO base card. The stock is young and this is its first rest under its post-listing high. Many IPO bases look like cups or flat bases, so the shape alone does not decide. The listing date does. A young listing has no 200-day, and that does not cancel the setup.
questions.lesson_line: Shape alone does not decide. A young stock's first rest is an IPO base.

wrong.The flat card: The shape can look flat, but the listing date decides. A young stock's first rest is an IPO base.
wrong.None; no 200-day: A young listing has no 200-day yet. That does not cancel the setup.
wrong.The VCP card: Nothing in the story shows shrinking swings. Tightening inside an IPO base is only a grade cue, not a VCP.

questions.story: The day before the breakout. A stock listed 68 sessions before the breakout rests 6.4 weeks, 12% deep, under its post-listing high. It is the first rest, and its numbers could pass for a flat base.
questions.simple: The IPO base card. The stock is young and this is its first rest, so the listing date decides, not the shape.

deeper.counter: Shape is not the label. While the stock is young, a rest that looks like a flat base is judged by the IPO base card. Past its first year, a stock is a regular base candidate and a different card judges it.

reasons: the window is a held decision, D-002
fixed before: story rewritten

questions.q: Which setup is it?
choices: A VCP, since the swings shrink
A bull flag, as it is a pause
An IPO base; tightening is a cue
A failed breakout, retesting
questions.answer: An IPO base; tightening is a cue
questions.why: An IPO base, and the tightening is only a grade cue. The stock is four months old and resting under its post-listing high, so the listing date decides. A young listing has no 200-day and one rest. Tightening inside an IPO base is a grade cue, not a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: Tightening inside an IPO base is a grade cue. It does not change the card.

wrong.A VCP, since the swings shrink: Tightening inside an IPO base is a grade cue, not a VCP. A young listing has no 200-day and one rest.
wrong.A failed breakout, retesting: Nothing has closed above the high, so there has been no breakout to fail. It is a first rest under the high.
wrong.A bull flag, as it is a pause: The story has no sharp run before the rest. It is a first rest under the post-listing high, and on a stock this young that is an IPO base.

questions.story: A stock listed four months ago rests under its highest price since listing for the first time. Nothing has closed above it. The weekly swings inside the rest get smaller each week.
questions.simple: It is an IPO base, because the stock is young and resting under its own high, and shrinking swings only help the grade.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line; the 200-day rule for young stocks is held (D-034)

questions.q: How does this base look?
choices: Weak; the V leaves no right side
Strong; buyers took it back
Strong; it is near the high
Weak; it must close above it
questions.answer: Weak; the V leaves no right side
questions.why: Weak. A fast V is a poor sign. The price ran from the low back to within 5% of the pivot in 5 sessions or fewer, with no pause. Here it went from 25% under the high to within 3% in four sessions. That leaves no right side to judge.
questions.lesson_line: A fast V straight into the pivot is a poor sign. It has no right side.

wrong.Strong; buyers took it back: A quick rebound looks bullish, but with no pause there is no quiet right side to judge.
wrong.Strong; it is near the high: Being near the high is only the end point. With no pause there was no right side to judge.
wrong.Weak; it must close above it: The trigger is a trade through the IPO high, not a close above it. It is weak because the V leaves no right side.

questions.story: A new issue drops 25% off its IPO high. Then in four sessions, with no pause, it climbs back within 3% of that high.
questions.simple: Weak. The price shot back up to the pivot in a few days with no pause, so there is no right side to judge.

deeper.trap: Being back near the high looks bullish. But a V in a few sessions leaves nothing to judge: no quiet pullbacks, no proof the sellers are done. A base earns its buy by resting, not by racing.

reasons: the V line is a proposed card line
the card also lists a fast V as a B- cue (c35): owner to rule which wins

questions.q: How do you handle the size?
choices: Fewer shares; size from the stop
Buy full size and skip the stop
Pull the stop in to 3% to keep size
Risk more to keep the same size
questions.answer: Fewer shares; size from the stop
questions.why: Fewer shares. Stop first, a few cents under the day's low. The size comes from the stop, so a wide honest stop means fewer shares. Shares equal account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down. This 28.70 stop sits 4.6% under the fill, inside the 5% we accept. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Never pull the stop in to fit the size. Cut the shares, or wait for a tighter trigger.

wrong.Pull the stop in to 3% to keep size: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is a trap. The honest stop stays.
wrong.Risk more to keep the same size: The size comes from the stop, not the other way round. A wide stop means fewer shares, not more risk.
wrong.Buy full size and skip the stop: With no stop there is no defined risk. The stop sets the size and is never skipped.

questions.story: Bought on the breakout at 30.09. The honest stop is 28.70, wider than the 1% to 3% we prefer.
questions.simple: Buy fewer shares. The stop sets the size, so a wide honest stop means a smaller position.

reasons: wide-stop sizing is tied to the held decision D-005
rests on the owner's rulebook, A3 and A5
fixed before: variety rewrite 2026-11-10

questions.q: What does the plan say at the open?
choices: Sell part at the open; it is the rule
Sell the whole position
Wait 30 minutes; it is the rule
Your call: sell part or hold on
questions.answer: Your call: sell part or hold on
questions.why: It is your call. 3R is 61.53 and the open at 62.00 is above it. It is day 4, so a sale is not too early. A gap past 3R is not an automatic sell. Selling part is one choice. Holding is another.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past your planned sell level is not an automatic sell. It is your call.

wrong.Sell the whole position: Too much at once. If you sell, sell part and keep the rest on the plan.
wrong.Sell part at the open; it is the rule: Selling part on a gap is one choice you may make. It is never a rule.
wrong.Wait 30 minutes; it is the rule: No rule makes you wait. The gap is past 3R, and what you do about it is your call.

questions.story: You bought at 57.42 with the stop at 56.05. The first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 at the earliest. On day 4 the stock opens at 62.00, above 3R at 61.53.
questions.simple: A gap past 3R is not an automatic sell. Selling part at the open is allowed, and so is holding.

deeper.example: Gaps skip levels. The open is above 3R, and it is day 4, so selling part is a fair choice. Holding for a longer push is a fair choice too. The gap is a chance to decide, not a rule to follow.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, F63 and B19
computed level, 61.53 is given in the story

questions.q: Which backdrop do new issues like best?
choices: A market turning up after a correction
A long, crowded advance for IPOs
A Red market with strong volume
A market that just started to fall
questions.answer: A market turning up after a correction
questions.why: A market turning up after a correction. That is a cue, not a rule. Be careful when the IPO calendar is crowded late in a long advance. IBD says new issues often pull back the hardest when the market stumbles into a correction. A weak market is no place for a new issue.
questions.lesson_line: New issues lead best out of a correction. Be careful when the calendar is crowded.

wrong.A long, crowded advance for IPOs: Be careful there. A crowded IPO calendar late in a long advance is a warning.
wrong.A Red market with strong volume: Red means mostly cash, and new issues often pull back the hardest when the market weakens.
wrong.A market that just started to fall: IBD says new issues often pull back the hardest when the market stumbles into a correction.

questions.simple: New issues do best when the market turns up after a correction. It is a cue, not a rule.

reasons: rests on the card's cue line
key was the longest choice before

questions.q: In our scan, most IPO base breakouts were stopped before reaching 3R.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. 36 of the 57 scan hits were stopped before 3R. The scan used a fixed stop and no trims, so it is a base rate, not a forecast for one trade. It is a probability trade. That is why we size from the stop and keep each loss small.
questions.lesson_line: Most IPO breakouts stop out first. Size from the stop and keep the losses small.
questions.simple: True. In our scan, 36 of the 57 IPO base hits were stopped before they reached 3R.

deeper.trap: Do not read a base rate as a promise. In the same scan 26.3% reached 3R and 17.5% reached 5R before the stop. The plan lives on small losses and on letting the few winners run.

reasons: a number from our own scan that changes when the scan is rerun
one source family, the research dossier

questions.q: Account 100,000, risk 0.5%, fill 54.72, stop 52.50. Ignore the position cap. How many shares?
questions.answer: 225 shares
questions.why: Risk dollars are the account times the risk percent: 100,000 times 0.5% is 500. Risk per share is the fill minus the stop, 54.72 minus 52.50. Divide 500 by that and round down to 225, never up. The size comes from the stop. Widening the stop to sit through the base's depth is a named mistake. In real life the position cap is checked too, and the smaller size wins.
questions.lesson_line: Shares come from the stop: risk in dollars divided by risk per share, rounded down.
questions.simple: The answer is 225 shares, because risk dollars divided by the risk per share, rounded down, gives the size.

deeper.trap: Rounding up gives one share too many. That share risks a few cents more than the dollars we planned. Round down, so the risk never goes past the limit.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, shares from the stop)

choices: 450 shares
500 shares
2,252 shares
225 shares

wrong.500 shares: That is the risk dollars read as shares. Divide by the risk per share.
wrong.2,252 shares: That risks ten times the planned dollars. A decimal slip.
wrong.450 shares: That risks double the planned dollars.

questions.story: Bought on the breakout.

questions.q: Which average is the default trail for a fast-moving new issue?
choices: The 200-day
The 50-day
The 9 EMA
The 20 EMA
questions.answer: The 9 EMA
questions.why: The 9 EMA. The default trail for a fast mover is the 9 EMA, and we sell on a close below it. Our card treats a new issue as a fast mover by default.
questions.lesson_line: A new issue is a fast mover by default: trail the 9 EMA and sell on a close below it.

wrong.The 50-day: The default trail for a fast mover is the 9 EMA, not the 50-day.
wrong.The 200-day: A young listing may not have a 200-day yet, and the default for a fast mover is the 9 EMA.
wrong.The 20 EMA: The 20 EMA is the trail for a steadier mover. A fast-moving new issue trails the 9 EMA.

questions.simple: The 9 EMA. A new issue is a fast mover by default, so we sell when the price closes below its 9 EMA.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, E52

questions.story: Bought on the breakout at 62.64 with the stop at 60.76.

questions.q: What is the plan?
choices: Sell it and free the money
Sell half now and hold the rest
Hold; the base was clean
Move the stop up to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell it and free the money
questions.why: Sell it and free the money. Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold. This one is up only 0.4R after 10 trading days. A clean base does not change the rule. The stop moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R, not at 0.4R.
questions.lesson_line: A trade that does nothing for 10 days is sold. Capital is for working trades.

wrong.Hold; the base was clean: The time stop does not care about the base. Under 1R after 10 days, we sell.
wrong.Sell half now and hold the rest: The time stop sells the whole trade. We sell part into strength, not into a stall at 0.4R.
wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, not at 0.4R. A trade under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

questions.story: You bought an IPO breakout 10 trading days ago. It has drifted sideways and is up only 0.4R.
questions.simple: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold to free the money.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, C33

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Skip it; that is the weekly limit
Take it; each trigger is a new trade
Take it at half size to be safe
Skip it; wait a month before trying
questions.answer: Skip it; that is the weekly limit
questions.why: Skip it. The same stock gets at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month. Three tries this week are used up, so a fourth is over the limit. A re-buy is always a new trade with its own stop and every rule, but the limit comes first.
questions.lesson_line: The same stock gets 3 tries a week and 6 a month. After that, skip it.

wrong.Take it; each trigger is a new trade: A new trigger is a new trade, but the same stock still gets at most 3 tries in a week.
wrong.Take it at half size to be safe: The limit is on tries, not size. A fourth try in the week is over it at any size.
wrong.Skip it; wait a month before trying: The limits are 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month. They are not a month-long wait.

questions.story: Three times this week you bought the same new issue's breakout and the stop took you out. A fourth trigger fires on Friday morning.
questions.simple: Skip it. The same stock gets at most 3 tries in a week, and you have used all three.

deeper.trap: Each stop-out was a planned loss. The pull is to try once more to win it back. The limit says no. Move on to the next setup.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B21 and E56

questions.q: After a stop-out we can buy the same stock again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, with its own stop and every rule. At most 3 tries in a week.
questions.lesson_line: A new buy is a new trade: new trigger, new stop, every rule again.

questions.q: Under our plan, what comes after the first sell?
choices: Sell it all at 5R and move on
Add more at 5R if it acts well
Sell more on strength, then trail
Hold the rest with no more sells
questions.answer: Sell more on strength, then trail
questions.why: Sell more on strength, then trail what is left. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. Later sells are a judgment too, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push or at about 5 to 10R.
questions.lesson_line: Sell into strength, then trail what is left.

wrong.Sell it all at 5R and move on: The plan keeps what is left on the trail instead of selling it all at one mark.
wrong.Add more at 5R if it acts well: Selling comes off, not on. The plan sells more into strength, then trails what is left.
wrong.Hold the rest with no more sells: Later sells are a judgment too. Holding everything with no more sells skips that step.

questions.simple: After the first sell, the plan sells more into strength and then trails what is left.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, B19)

questions.q: What does our rule say to do with your long?
choices: Sell a big part into the gap
Add a little on the gap up
Hold it all and trail the 9 EMA
Raise the stop and sell nothing
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the gap
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run on your own long is a judgment call, and our rule is to sell a big part into the strength. This one fits: 400% in seven weeks, then a gap up on huge volume. The rest stays on the trail, and the stop only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: When a new issue goes parabolic, sell a big part into the strength.

wrong.Add a little on the gap up: A climax run on your own long is when we sell a big part into it, not when we buy more.
wrong.Raise the stop and sell nothing: Raising the stop is fine, but on a climax run the plan is to sell a big part, not only to tighten the stop.
wrong.Hold it all and trail the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA trail is the exit for what is left. A climax run is a reason to sell a big part first.

questions.story: Your new-issue long has run 400% in seven weeks. Today it gaps up again on huge volume.
questions.simple: Sell a big part into the burst, because on a climax run our rule is to sell into strength.

deeper.trap: A big part is not all of it. The rule calls it a judgment call, so the size of the sale is yours to weigh. The rest still trails under the 9 EMA for a fast mover, and a close below it is the exit.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, 'yes but depends')

questions.q: What fails this base?
choices: It sank under the first day's open
It broke out through the IPO high
The first day opened too high
It is a new issue on its first base
questions.answer: It sank under the first day's open
questions.why: It sank under the first day's open. IBD and MarketSmith India want a base to hold above the IPO price, and for a direct listing the first open stands in for it. This base sank to 135.51, under the 165.90 open. SPOT undercut its opening price by 18% and its breakout reached 0.0R.
questions.lesson_line: A base that sinks under the IPO price has a hole in its floor.

wrong.It broke out through the IPO high: Trading through the IPO high is the trigger, not a flaw. The fault is the base before it.
wrong.It is a new issue on its first base: A new issue's first base is what this card covers. The fault is the floor under it.
wrong.The first day opened too high: A high open is not a flaw. The fault is the later low, which sank under it.

questions.story: The day before the trigger. A direct listing opened at 165.90 on its first day. Its first base sank to a low of 135.51. The next day it trades through its IPO high.
questions.simple: The base failed because it sank under the first day's open, and a good base holds above the IPO price.

deeper.trap: Do not judge the floor by the breakout alone. A stock can clear its IPO high after the base has already broken its floor. Check the base low against the IPO price before you look at volume or the trigger.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-057: which price counts as the IPO price)
fixed before

questions.q: Which card judges it now?
choices: No card; skip it, it is too old
The IPO base card, it listed lately
A regular base, on its own rules
The IPO base card, it lacks a 200-day
questions.answer: A regular base, on its own rules
questions.why: A regular base. The stock is past its first year, so the IPO base card no longer applies. The breakout came 318 sessions after listing, far past the card's first-year cutoff. The shelf itself is clean. Only the card changes.
questions.lesson_line: Past the first year, an IPO base turns into a regular base.

wrong.No card; skip it, it is too old: The base can still be good. It just needs the right card.
wrong.The IPO base card, it listed lately: 318 sessions is past a year. The IPO base card has timed out.
wrong.The IPO base card, it lacks a 200-day: At 318 sessions the stock is old enough for a 200-day. Its age, not its averages, decides the card.

questions.story: The day before the breakout. A clean 3.6-week, 14% shelf under the high breaks out on 2.2x volume the next day. The breakout comes 318 sessions after listing.
questions.simple: A regular base, because the stock is past its first year, so the IPO base card no longer applies.

deeper.example: CAVA is the case. It was a clean 3.6-week, 14% shelf on 2.2x volume. But it came 318 sessions after listing, past its first year. The shelf was fine. Only the card was wrong.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-002: the first-year window)

questions.q: How strong is this breakout?
choices: Strong; spin-offs run
Strong; the base was tight
Weak; the base was too deep
Weak; no demand on the day
questions.answer: Weak; no demand on the day
questions.why: Weak. The breakout traded 0.75x the base's average volume, which is below average. IBD wants heavy volume on the breakout day and week. For us volume raises the grade, so this one grades weak. It does not cancel the setup. The spin-off label and the shallow base do not change that. This one's best was 0.82R.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout on below-average volume grades weak: little demand on the day.

wrong.Strong; the base was tight: A tight base helps, but the breakout day still needs buyers.
wrong.Strong; spin-offs run: Being a spin-off does not make a breakout strong. The volume on the day does.
wrong.Weak; the base was too deep: A 10% base is shallow. IBD says most IPO bases correct less than 20%, so depth is not the problem.

questions.story: The breakout day. A spin-off listed in June. A 6-week, 10% base at the high breaks out today on 0.75x the base's average volume.
questions.simple: Weak, because the breakout came on less volume than the base averaged, so buyers were not there.

deeper.trap: Do not read a clean base as proof of demand. NWSA had a 6-week, 10% base at the high, yet the breakout came on 0.75x the base's volume. Volume is the demand check, and here it graded the breakout weak. A weak grade is not a ban.

reasons: rests on held decisions (D-006: volume as a gate or a cue; D-054: spin-offs)

questions.q: What went wrong?
choices: The stop should have been wider
Nothing; the stop did its job
We should have skipped the breakout
questions.answer: Nothing; the stop did its job
questions.why: Nothing went wrong. The honest stop was 6.7% away and sized for it. The trade reached 0.6R and fell to the stop four sessions later. That is a planned loss.
questions.lesson_line: A wide honest stop is sized in shares. When it hits, the loss is the plan.

wrong.The stop should have been wider: Widening the stop is a named mistake. It only grows the loss.
wrong.We should have skipped the breakout: Every rule passed, and the size was set from the stop. Skipping it afterwards is hindsight.

questions.story: MDB: a 20% base on 1.8x volume. The honest stop is 6.7% under the fill. It reaches 0.6R, then falls to the stop four sessions later.

questions.q: What does a Yellow reading change?
choices: Full risk on clean bases
Smaller and fewer positions
Only A+ setups
Mostly cash and shorts, no longs
questions.answer: Smaller and fewer positions
questions.why: Smaller and fewer positions. Under our market reading, Green is full risk and Yellow is smaller and fewer. Orange is only A+ setups. Red is mostly cash and shorts. APTV broke out twice on clean bases in a flat 2012 market, the second on 2.8x volume, and stopped out both times. The Yellow reading is this story's own.
questions.lesson_line: In a flat market, clean bases still fail. Yellow means smaller and fewer.

wrong.Full risk on clean bases: Full risk is the Green reading, not Yellow.
wrong.Only A+ setups: That is Orange. Yellow means smaller and fewer, not A+ only.
wrong.Mostly cash and shorts, no longs: That is Red. Yellow means smaller and fewer positions, not mostly cash.

questions.story: The day before its second breakout. The first base broke out in February and stopped out. The market has been flat all year, and your market reading says Yellow.
questions.simple: Yellow means we take smaller and fewer positions. It does not mean full risk, and it is not the Orange rule of only A+ setups.

deeper.trap: A clean base does not make the market Green. APTV's two clean-looking failures came in a flat 2012 market. Read the market first, then the chart.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65 market reading)

questions.q: Was the setup wrong?
choices: No; the loss is planned
Yes; the base was too short
Yes; the stop was too tight
questions.answer: No; the loss is planned
questions.why: No. Every rule passed and the stop was set before the buy. NAVN broke out on 2.1x volume, closed near the high, and fell through the stop the next session.
questions.lesson_line: A clean setup can still lose. The stop is the cost of finding out.

wrong.Yes; the base was too short: A short base is fine for a new issue. The loss is not proof the rule failed.
wrong.Yes; the stop was too tight: The stop was the honest one. Widening it after the fact only grows the loss.

questions.story: NAVN: a 2-week, 7% shelf at the IPO high breaks out on 2.1x volume and closes near its high. Next session it falls through the 4.6% stop.

questions.q: Two IPO bases are otherwise similar. Which one grades higher on depth?
choices: The 12% deep base, it fell less
The 33% deep base, it has more upside
Neither; depth does not grade
The base with the longer rest
questions.answer: The 12% deep base, it fell less
questions.why: The 12% deep base. Shallower bases grade higher. IBD says most IPO bases correct less than 20%. Grading is a judgment call, so depth is one sign among several.
questions.lesson_line: Shallower bases grade higher. Depth is one sign, and grading stays a judgment call.

wrong.Neither; depth does not grade: Depth is one of the signs. It helps decide the grade.
wrong.The 33% deep base, it has more upside: A deeper fall grades lower, not higher. Shallower bases grade higher.
wrong.The base with the longer rest: Length is a separate sign. This question asks about depth, and the shallower base grades higher.

questions.story: Two IPO bases are otherwise similar. One is 12% deep. The other is 33% deep.
questions.simple: The shallower base grades higher, because a smaller fall from the high is a healthier sign.

deeper.trap: Do not treat a grade line as a gate. The rulebook says grading is discretionary, with no fixed checklist taught as ours. Depth moves the grade. It does not decide it alone.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-055: the depth cap and grade lines)
fixed before

questions.q: A steady mover late in its first year. Which trail?
choices: The 21-day
The 10-day
The listing-day low
questions.answer: The 21-day
questions.why: The 21-day. SABR was a steady mover late in its first year, and the 21-day trail fit it better than the 10-day.
questions.lesson_line: Steady mover, 21-day trail. Fast mover, 10-day trail.

wrong.The 10-day: That is the default for fast movers. A steady mover gets shaken out of it.
wrong.The listing-day low: That is a level to watch, not a trail.

questions.q: Was the breakout buyable?
choices: Yes, it cleared the IPO high
Yes, if you use a tight stop
No; too stretched and past 4%
No; it needs a close above first
questions.answer: No; too stretched and past 4%
questions.why: No. We skip a long more than 10% above its 9 EMA, and this one opens 18% over it. It also opens 12% above the IPO high, past the 4% chase limit. Skip it and wait for a new setup. Clearing the high or a tighter stop does not change the rule.
questions.lesson_line: A gap-and-go is not a buy. Skip it and let the next setup come.

Base B: buyers show up when it rises

A good sign; it replaces the trigger

questions.q: Which base does our card end before the trigger?
choices: Only B, which never got back above
Both, since each undercut the price
Neither, since no trigger has fired
Neither; undercuts just lower a grade
questions.answer: Only B, which never got back above
questions.why: Only B. Our card ends a base when the low undercuts the IPO price and does not close back above it within 3 sessions. Stock A closed at $16.10 one session after its dip. questions.simple: Only B, because our card ends a base that stays under the IPO price for more than 3 sessions.

wrong.Both, since each undercut the price: Our card gives an undercut 3 sessions to close back above the IPO price. Stock A did it in one, so this check does not end its base.
wrong.Neither, since no trigger has fired: This check runs before the trigger. A base can end before it ever breaks out.
wrong.Neither; undercuts just lower a grade: Stock B did not close back above the price within 3 sessions. On our card that ends the base.

deeper.trap: The 3-session window is our card's proposal, not a source's. MarketSmith India wants no undercut at all. Stock A's close of $16.10 sits above the offer, the open and the day-one close, so the call holds whichever one counts.

questions.q: A new issue closes above its IPO AVWAP. What does that tell you?
choices: The average buyer is ahead
The stock has cleared its IPO high
Volume is drying up on the pullbacks
The average buyer is underwater
questions.answer: The average buyer is ahead
questions.why: The average buyer is ahead. The IPO AVWAP is the volume-weighted average price anchored at the listing day. It is roughly what the typical share since listing cost. A close above it means that buyer is in profit. Our card checks that the close sits above it. The buy still waits for the trade through the IPO high.
questions.lesson_line: Above the IPO AVWAP, the average buyer since listing is in profit.

wrong.The stock has cleared its IPO high: No. The AVWAP is an average price, not the high. The pivot is the IPO high.
wrong.Volume is drying up on the pullbacks: The AVWAP uses volume to weight the average. It does not say if volume is drying up.
wrong.The average buyer is underwater: That is backwards. Above the average price means the average buyer is in profit.

questions.simple: The IPO AVWAP is the average price paid since listing, weighted by volume, so a close above it means the average buyer is ahead.
